passage: Ishita, I saw your face at the Diwali dinner when Aunty announced your cousin's marks and then asked what you'd got. I'm Pranav, your Mama, and I remember that hot, sinking feeling. At your age I was the one compared aloud to my elder brother, in front of half our relatives. I went red and stared at my plate. What I understood later was that my mother's pride and worry were leaking out of her, and I happened to be standing there. It was never about my worth. So talk to your mother privately, not at the party. Tell her it hurts to be measured out loud. Then show her your effort your own way. I'll be nearby if you'd like company.

qa.q: Who announced the cousin's marks at the Diwali dinner?
What did young Pranav feel when he was compared aloud to his brother?
qa.a: He felt ashamed, hot and sinking, going red and staring at his plate while being judged in front of relatives.

qa.q: What could Ishita do about being compared at family gatherings?
qa.a: Ishita can ask their mother privately to stop measuring them out loud, and show effort in their own way.

qa.q: How might Ishita's mother feel about the comparison at the dinner?
qa.a: Her pride and anxiety were probably driving it, so she may not realise how much it stings, which is why a private talk could help. 🤍

grounding: Shows an elder telling a teen about being compared aloud, that it comes from adults' pride and anxiety, and advising a private request to stop.

passage:
At Bhavna didi's engagement, the banquet hall was so loud Aadhya could barely hear herself think. Then, at the long dinner table, Mummy's voice cut through: "Bhavna got 96 in boards. Aadhya, only 74. What will we do with her?" Twelve relatives looked at her. An uncle laughed. Aadhya stared at her paneer, cheeks burning. It wasn't her fault that Mummy got nervous around her sisters, but it felt like it was.
She didn't argue in front of everyone. Later, while the band played, she found Mummy by the dessert counter. "Mummy, please don't compare my marks in front of the family. I feel judged by everyone. I'm working on maths. I went from 58 to 74. That's my progress."
Mummy blinked. "I just get nervous when my sisters start boasting." She squeezed Aadhya's hand. "From 58 to 74. I'll say that next time."

qa.q: What mark was Aadhya's compared with Bhavna's 96?
How did Aadhya feel when twelve relatives looked at her?
qa.a: Judged and ashamed; her cheeks burned.

qa.q: How did Aadhya handle it wisely?
qa.a: She did not argue in public, then privately asked Mummy to stop comparing and pointed to her own progress from 58 to 74.
Her own nerves and pride when her sisters start boasting.

grounding: A teenager compared aloud at a family gathering feels judged, sees the parent's anxiety as the source, and privately asks her to stop while showing her own progress.

passage:
Every Diwali at Nani's Mumbai flat, Papa played the same game. "Ankita has three swimming medals now. Seema, what do you have?" This year he said it while the whole family was lighting diyas on the balcony. Aunties made sympathetic noises. Ankita, holding the matchbox, looked as awkward as Seema felt.
Seema's face went hot. She thought of the sketchbook under her bed, full of drawings nobody asked about. None of this was her fault. Papa always got loud when his elder brother was around.
She waited until the next morning, when Papa was alone with his tea. "Papa, when you compare me with Ankita in front of everyone, I feel small. Please stop. I'm not a swimmer. But the school has picked three of my drawings for the art exhibition."
Papa's cup stopped halfway. "Three? Why didn't you tell me?"
"You never asked," she said quietly.
He put the cup down. "I'm asking now."

qa.q: How many swimming medals does Ankita have?
How did Seema feel when Papa asked what she had?
qa.a: Judged and small; her face went hot in front of the family.

qa.q: What did Seema do to handle the pressure?
qa.a: She waited to speak to Papa alone, asked him to stop comparing, and shared her own achievement on her own terms.

qa.q: How did Ankita seem to feel during the comparison?
qa.a: Awkward, just like Seema, standing there holding the matchbox.

grounding: A teenager compared aloud at a family gathering feels judged, asks her parent privately to stop and shows her effort on her own terms.
